title: Blueberries and the Brain: What a 24-Week Clinical Trial in Older Adults Found
metaDescription: A randomized clinical trial with 57 older adults evaluated freeze-dried blueberry and brain health. We tell you what was observed and what was not.
excerpt: A double-blind trial with 57 older adults tested 20 g a day of freeze-dried blueberry for 24 weeks. Here are its results and how to interpret them with caution.
imageAlt: Fresh high-mountain blueberries on a light surface, in natural light

blocks.text: Introduction: what happens in the brain when we eat blueberries?

Blueberries have earned a reputation as allies of memory and healthy aging, mostly because of their anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their deep blue color. But reputation is one thing and what well-controlled clinical trials show is another. A study published in August 2026 in the journal Clinical Nutrition ESPEN tests that idea with a rigorous design, and its main result is a good reminder of how nutrition science works: sometimes the answer is “no effect was observed”.

A team of researchers from Mass General Brigham, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School recruited 57 older people without cognitive problems. The average age was around 73. Of them, 28 received 20 grams of freeze-dried blueberry powder every day and 29 received an identical-looking placebo, for 24 weeks. Neither the participants nor the researchers knew who was getting what, which is known as a double-blind design.

The main goal was to measure whether blueberry powder reduced two blood markers associated with brain health: phosphorylated tau protein (p-tau181) and neurofilament light chain (NFL). Every eight weeks blood samples were taken and computer-based cognitive tests were given. As secondary goals, other blood markers and blood pressure were measured.

items: There were no statistically significant differences between the two groups in p-tau181 or NFL after 24 weeks.
No effects were observed either on the cognitive tests, systolic blood pressure or the other markers measured.
A reduction in diastolic blood pressure was observed in the group that consumed blueberry, a secondary finding.

blocks.text: The authors themselves conclude that 24 weeks of freeze-dried blueberry had no effect on p-tau181 or NFL in older adults. It is an honest and useful result: it indicates that, with this dose, this duration and this group of people, the expected effect on those markers did not appear.

Several limitations should be kept in mind. The study is small, with 57 participants, and the volunteers were cognitively healthy people, in whom brain markers change little in just six months. In addition, freeze-dried blueberry powder was used, not fresh fruit, and only one dose. A no-effect result in this design does not mean blueberries are harmful or that they offer nothing: it means this specific study did not find the change it was looking for.

The finding on diastolic pressure is interesting, but since it is a secondary result in a small group it should be taken with caution and needs to be confirmed in larger studies before drawing conclusions.

The practical lesson is simple: no single food is a solution for the brain. What healthy eating guidelines do support is an eating pattern with plenty of fruits and vegetables, fiber and minimally processed foods, together with physical activity, good sleep and social life. Blueberries fit very well in that pattern because they are a fruit rich in fiber and water, with a natural sweet taste and very easy to incorporate.

items: Add them to breakfast with oats or plain yogurt.
Use them as a fresh snack instead of ultra-processed snacks.
Combine them with salads, smoothies or homemade desserts with little added sugar.

blocks.text: Good science also includes no-effect results, and this study is an example of how knowledge is built little by little. While more research arrives, blueberries remain a delicious way to add fruit to your day.
